title: Language Models Need Sleep: Learning to Self-Modify and Consolidate Memories
authors: Ali Behrouz (Google), Farnoosh Hashemi (Cornell), Vahab Mirrokni (Google)
date: arXiv v1: 2 June 2026 (paper states a version has been publicly available on OpenReview since September 2025)
tldr: This paper argues that a continual-learning LLM should not have a train/test split at all, but a periodic wake/sleep lifecycle: during 'wake' the model ingests data through a Nested-Learning-style Continuum Memory System (a chain of MLP blocks each updated at its own, progressively slower frequency), and during 'sleep' it stops taking input and runs two offline processes. First, Memory Consolidation: just before a fast memory block's parameters would be overwritten by its own scheduled update, its knowledge is distilled 'upward' (Knowledge Seeding) into freshly activated low-rank MoE experts added to the next slower block, using Generalized Knowledge Distillation plus an RL 'Learning to Imitate' reward, after which the fast block's previously-added experts are reset (synaptic pruning). Second, Dreaming: a SEAL-style RL loop in which the model generates synthetic data with deliberately randomized MoE routing for novelty, filters dreams by a gradient-based importance score, LoRA-fine-tunes on each surviving dream, and reinforces the dream-generation policy with ReST^EM. Experiments on continual class-incremental learning, long-context benchmarks (near-perfect BABILong up to 10M tokens), SQuAD knowledge incorporation (beats SEAL), ARC few-shot (80% vs SEAL's 72.5%), and math reasoning (Qwen3-8B AIME-24 79.2 vs GRPO 76.4) support the two-stage design.
problem_and_motivation: The paper attacks the static-after-deployment nature of LLMs. Once pre-/post-training ends, knowledge lives in exactly two places: (1) the immediate context window, via in-context learning (ICL), which is erased at the end of every session; and (2) frozen MLP/projection weights, which encode only pre-cutoff knowledge. The authors reuse Behrouz et al.'s (Nested Learning) analogy to anterograde amnesia: like a patient who cannot form new long-term memories, a deployed LLM perpetually experiences the present as new because nothing bridges short-term (context) and long-term (weights) memory. Existing remedies fail on one horn or the other of a dilemma: re-pretraining is prohibitively expensive for frequent updates, while continual fine-tuning / LoRA updates cause catastrophic forgetting (CF). The Nested Learning (NL) paradigm and its Hope architecture already provide what the authors call ONLINE consolidation: a Continuum Memory System (CMS) in which components update at different frequencies during the active phase, transferring knowledge from fast to slow blocks end-to-end. But the paper identifies three gaps in online-only consolidation: it keeps knowledge at the same level of abstraction (no lossy compression, so it consumes the same capacity); it is selective and retrieval-dependent (strengthens only what is actively recalled); and it is context-bound (misses higher-level integration of new knowledge with existing knowledge). Drawing on the neuroscience of sleep — NREM/slow-wave sleep performing hippocampus-to-neocortex memory consolidation plus synaptic homeostasis (global downscaling), and REM sleep performing synapse strengthening, integration, and future-scenario simulation via dreaming — the paper proposes an OFFLINE consolidation phase ('Sleep') for LLMs and asserts a paradigm claim: for a continual learner there is no training or test time, only alternating active/wake phases (new input arrives) and sleep phases (no external input; internal processing to consolidate memories and self-improve). CF is reframed as fundamentally a capacity problem — parameters must be overwritten to fit new knowledge — whose biological solution is neuroplasticity, motivating gradual parameter expansion rather than regularization (EWC-style) or rehearsal alone.
core_mechanism:
SUBSTRATE: CONTINUUM MEMORY SYSTEM (CMS), imported from Nested Learning. The backbone block is a sequence-mixing layer (attention or any recurrent/test-time-memory module) followed by a chain of k MLP blocks $\mathrm{MLP}^{(f_1)}(\cdot),\dots,\mathrm{MLP}^{(f_k)}(\cdot)$, each with its own update frequency. Definition 1 (update frequency): for a weight component $W$, its frequency $f_W$ is its number of updates per unit of time, where the unit of time is one update step of the SLOWEST module. (Canonical example: in a fast-weight programmer over a length-$L$ sequence, the fast weights update $L$ times per slow-weight step, so $f=L$; attention is the $f\to\infty$ extreme, a frozen pre-trained MLP the $f=0$ extreme.) Each block $\ell$ has chunk size $C^{(\ell)} := \max_{\ell'} C^{(\ell')}/f_\ell$, and WLOG $C^{(\ell)}$ is divisible by $C^{(\ell-1)}$. The forward pass (Eq. 1, normalizations omitted) is $y_t = \mathrm{MLP}^{(f_k)}(\mathrm{MLP}^{(f_{k-1})}(\cdots \mathrm{MLP}^{(f_1)}(x_t)))$ where $x=\{x_1,\dots,x_T\}$, $x\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d_{in}}$ is the input sequence of length $L$ (the paper also uses $T$). Parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(f_\ell)}$ of block $\ell$ update every $C^{(\ell)}$ steps: $\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(f_\ell)}_{i+1} = \boldsymbol{\theta}^{(f_\ell)}_i - \boldsymbol{e}_{i,\ell}$ with (Eq. 2) $\boldsymbol{e}_{i,\ell} = \sum_{t=i-C^{(\ell)}}^{i} \eta_t^{(\ell)}\, f(\boldsymbol{\theta}_t^{(f_\ell)}; x_t)$ if $i \equiv 0 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ C^{(\ell)})$, and $\boldsymbol{e}_{i,\ell}=0$ otherwise. Here $\eta_t^{(\ell)}$ are learning rates for $\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(f_\ell)}$ and $f(\cdot)$ is the error component of an ARBITRARY optimizer (e.g., $\nabla\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_t^{(f_\ell)}; x_t)$ for gradient descent) inside end-to-end optimization of the network; the objective $\mathcal{L}$ is task-dependent. Interpretation: each block compresses its own chunk of context into its parameters — earlier (high-frequency) blocks are short-term memory, later (low-frequency) blocks are long-term memory. With one MLP block and $f=0$ this degenerates to a standard Transformer, so CMS is a strict superset. WHY: multi-frequency updates postpone CF, but CF still strikes whenever update periods of all blocks align — hence the need for a consolidation mechanism that fires BEFORE each block's parameters get overwritten.

SLEEP SCHEDULING. Given chunk lengths $\{C^{(1)},\dots,C^{(k)}\}$, sleep (and thus memory consolidation) occurs exactly at steps $\{C^{(1)}\times b,\dots,C^{(k)}\times b\}$ for all $b\in\mathbb{N}$ — i.e., at every scheduled update boundary of every block, consolidate that block's knowledge into its slower neighbor first. Because frequencies are nested (e.g., $f=1\mathrm{K}$ feeding $f=10\mathrm{K}$), the fast block is consolidated into the slow block multiple times (10 times in that example) before the slow block's own update — repeated writes into a fixed-size slow memory are exactly where CF would occur, motivating expansion.

STAGE 1a: PARAMETER EXPANSION (periodic parameter (de)activation). WLOG each $\mathrm{MLP}^{(f_\ell)}$ is a sparse mixture-of-experts with router $\mathcal{R}^{(f_\ell)}$ and experts $\{W^{(f_\ell),1},\dots,W^{(f_\ell),s_\ell}\}$, $s_\ell \ge 1$ the current expert count. Let $\ell^*-1$ be the block being consolidated into block $\ell^*$. To avoid interference between transferred and existing knowledge in $\mathrm{MLP}^{(f_{\ell^*})}$, a NEW low-rank expert is appended: an MLP parameterized by $\{\mathbf{A}^{(f_{\ell^*}),s_{\ell^*}+1}, \mathbf{B}^{(f_{\ell^*}),s_{\ell^*}+1}\}$ with $\mathbf{A}^{(f_{\ell^*})} \in \mathbb{R}^{d\times d_{low}}$, $\mathbf{B}^{(f_{\ell^*})} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{low}\times d}$, $d_{low} \ll d$. Only these new parameters receive the transferred knowledge; after each sleep, a subset of layers has grown. Implementation note (important for infra): rather than dynamically resizing tensors, ALL prospective experts are allocated at initialization and masked in forward and backward passes until their activation during some sleep stage — static shapes, no recompilation; the analogy given is that the brain has fixed capacity and 'unlocks' neurons by forming new connections.

STAGE 1b: KNOWLEDGE SEEDING (KS) — UPWARD DISTILLATION. Definition: given small models $\mathcal{S}_1(\cdot),\dots,\mathcal{S}_k(\cdot)$ as teacher(s), KS transfers their knowledge into a LARGER model $\mathcal{M}(\cdot)$. Self-Knowledge Seeding (SKS) is the special case where the teacher is a smaller version of the SAME model: let $\mathrm{LM}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}$ be the model BEFORE expansion (teacher) and $\mathrm{LM}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}_{exp}}$ the model AFTER (i) parameter expansion and (ii) the Eq.-2 update of $\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(f_{\ell^*-1})}$ (student). Two challenges distinguish this from ordinary distillation: (1) the student has MORE capacity/expressive power than the teacher, so training on a fixed teacher-generated dataset (sequence-level KD a la Kim & Rush 2016) underuses student parameters; (2) the model is asleep — no external data — so classic Hinton-style KD on a held corpus is unavailable. The fix builds on Generalized Knowledge Distillation (GKD, Agarwal et al. 2024). A dataset $\mathcal{D}$ is constructed by SAMPLING FROM THE TEACHER $\mathrm{LM}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}$. The on-policy distillation objective is $\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{exp}) = (1-\lambda)\,\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}}\big[\mathcal{F}(\mathrm{LM}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \| \mathrm{LM}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}_{exp}})(y|x)\big] + \lambda\,\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\big[\mathbb{E}_{y\sim \mathrm{LM}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}_{exp}}(\cdot|x)}[\mathcal{F}(\mathrm{LM}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \| \mathrm{LM}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}_{exp}})(y|x)]\big]$, where $\mathcal{F}$ is a divergence between teacher and student token distributions and $\lambda\in[0,1]$ sets the fraction of on-policy, student-generated rollouts (the student receives token-level feedback from teacher logits on its OWN generations). Two deliberate restrictions: no backpropagation through the student's sampling distribution (stability + speed), and ALL student parameters are frozen EXCEPT the newly expanded low-rank expert — so transferred knowledge physically cannot overwrite old knowledge (structural CF prevention rather than regularization).

STAGE 1c: LEARNING TO IMITATE (LTI). Empirical observation motivating it: after distillation the student 'has' the knowledge but only weakly mimics the teacher's sampling/behavior — knowing vs using. LTI adds RL: from teacher-generated data (dreams) $\mathcal{D}_T=\{d^{(1)},\dots,d^{(n)}\}$, sample a random prefix of each $d^{(i)}$, have the student complete it as $\hat{d}^{(i)}$, and reward (Eq. 3) $r(\hat{d}^{(i)}; d^{(i)}; \mathrm{LM}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}_{exp}}) = \gamma\, r_{sem}(\hat{d}^{(i)}; d^{(i)}; \mathrm{LM}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}_{exp}}) + (1-\gamma)\, r_{abs}(\hat{d}^{(i)}; d^{(i)}; \mathrm{LM}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}_{exp}})$ with mixing weight $\gamma$. Semantic reward $r_{sem}$: a FROZEN reward model outputs 1 if $\hat{d}^{(i)}$ and $d^{(i)}$ are semantically equivalent, else 0. Absolute reward $r_{abs}$ (Eq. 4), with $z(\cdot,\cdot)$ the Levenshtein distance and threshold $z_0$: $r_{abs} = 1 - z(\hat{d}^{(i)}, d^{(i)}) / \max\{|\hat{d}^{(i)}|, |d^{(i)}|\}$ if $z(\hat{d}^{(i)}, d^{(i)}) \le z_0$, else $0$. The combined Knowledge Seeding objective (to be maximized over the expanded parameters) is $\mathcal{L}_{KS}(\boldsymbol{\theta}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{exp}) = \mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\big[(1-\alpha)\,\mathbb{E}_{y\sim \mathrm{LM}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}_{exp}}(\cdot|x)}[r(y)] - \alpha\,\mathbb{E}_{y\sim \mathrm{LM}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}_{exp}}(\cdot|x)}[\mathcal{D}(\mathrm{LM}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \| \mathrm{LM}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}_{exp}})(y|x)]\big]$, where $\alpha\in[0,1]$ trades distillation strength (divergence penalty $\mathcal{D}$) against the LTI reward term. After consolidation completes, ALL low-rank experts previously added (in past sleeps) to the FASTER block $\mathrm{MLP}^{(f_{\ell^*-1})}$ are RESET, freeing its capacity for future wake phases — the paper's analog of synaptic pruning. Net invariant: fast memories stay small and plastic; slow memories grow monotonically in (pre-allocated) capacity and are only ever written through fresh low-rank experts.

STAGE 2: DREAMING (REM analog, self-modification). Any self-improvement synthetic-data method can plug in; the proof of concept builds on SEAL (Zweiger et al. 2025) but fixes three of its problems for the continual setting: (1) SEAL's inner-loop SFT cost limits it to few self-edits; (2) iterative self-improvement causes CF (which stage 1 mitigates by consolidating BEFORE dreaming modifies the model); (3) SEAL samples only from the model's existing knowledge distribution, whereas dreaming should explore NOVEL syntheses of memories. Procedure, given a sampled task $(C,\tau)$ where $C$ is a context with task-relevant information and $\tau(\cdot)$ a downstream performance measure: (i) generate $m\ge 1$ dreams $\{\mathrm{DREAM}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^m \sim \mathrm{LM}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\cdot|C)$, where during sampling EVERY MoE router additionally activates one RANDOM expert, deliberately injecting irrelevant knowledge so the model can surface latent cross-memory patterns (the novelty mechanism replacing SEAL's pure self-sampling); (ii) reject most dreams via gradient-based data selection: each dream gets importance score $\boldsymbol{\omega}^{(i)}$ from the gradient of the language-modeling objective, $g_{DR}^{(i)} = \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \mathcal{L}_{SFT}(\mathrm{DREAM}^{(i)}, \boldsymbol{\theta})$, and the Top-$k$ dreams by score are kept PLUS $b$ random dreams for diversity, giving selected set $\mathrm{D}$; (iii) for each $\mathrm{DREAM}^{(i)} \in \mathrm{D}$, an ISOLATED instance of the model is fine-tuned with LoRA: $\boldsymbol{\theta}'^{(i)} \leftarrow \mathrm{SFT}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(i)}, \mathrm{DREAM}^{(i)})$; (iv) the GENERATION of the dream is rewarded by whether it helped (Eq. 5): $r(\mathrm{DREAM}^{(i)}, \tau(\cdot), \mathrm{LM}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(i)}}) = 1$ if $\mathrm{LM}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}'^{(i)}}$ improves over $\mathrm{LM}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(i)}}$ on $\tau$, else 0; (v) the dream-generation policy is optimized with the ReST^EM algorithm (Singh et al. 2024), following SEAL. WHY the two-stage order matters: consolidation first parks fragile new knowledge in freshly expanded, otherwise-frozen slow parameters, so the destructive weight updates of iterative self-training (the collapse/forgetting failure modes reported for OPSD-style pipelines) cannot erode it.
outer_loop_training:
This paper is unusual within the TTT/neural-memory line: it explicitly REJECTS the outer/inner (train/test) dichotomy — its central claim is that a continual learner has only wake and sleep phases. Still, three distinct optimization regimes map onto what this study series calls the outer loop.

(1) BASE PRE-TRAINING OF THE BACKBONE. Experiments start from conventionally pre-trained checkpoints (Llama-3B/8B, Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen3-1.7B/8B) or from the Hope architecture of Nested Learning. For Hope/CMS, pre-training is end-to-end: gradients flow through the multi-frequency CMS updates of Eq. 2, meaning the outer optimization shapes the blocks so that their inner (chunk-cadenced) self-updates compress context usefully — exactly the meta-learning-through-inner-loop structure of TTT/Titans, generalized to a whole chain of frequencies. The paper itself does not re-derive this training; it inherits it from Nested Learning, and the chunk structure of Eq. 2 IS the parallelization hook: block $\ell$'s error term is a plain accumulation $\sum_{t=i-C^{(\ell)}}^{i} \eta_t^{(\ell)} f(\boldsymbol{\theta}_t^{(f_\ell)}; x_t)$ applied once per $C^{(\ell)}$ tokens, so within a chunk the parameters are constant and the whole chunk can be processed in parallel with one deferred update — the same chunkwise trick that makes DeltaNet/TTT training feasible, here applied per frequency level (the companion TNT paper, arXiv:2511.07343, is dedicated to making exactly this chunkwise training efficient). For readers from inference backgrounds: this needs scaffolding on (a) what it means to backpropagate THROUGH an optimizer step (treat the update rule as a differentiable layer), and (b) why chunking converts a sequential recurrence of weight updates into batched matmuls.

(2) SLEEP-TIME CONSOLIDATION OPTIMIZATION (Knowledge Seeding). This is a genuine gradient-based training procedure, but run periodically during the model's deployed life rather than once before it. Trainable parameters: ONLY the newly activated low-rank expert $\{\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{B}\}$ in the target slow block; everything else frozen. Objective: $\mathcal{L}_{KS}$ combining the GKD divergence term (mixture of teacher-data and on-policy student-rollout divergences, controlled by $\lambda$ and $\alpha$) and the LTI policy-gradient reward term ($\gamma$-weighted semantic reward from a frozen reward model + Levenshtein reward). Notably, gradients do NOT flow through the student's sampling distribution — a deliberate biased-but-stable choice (standard practice inherited from GKD) that also avoids REINFORCE-style variance on the divergence term. Data: entirely self-generated (teacher = the smaller pre-expansion self), no external corpus.

(3) DREAMING OPTIMIZATION. Two nested optimizations: per-dream LoRA SFT (inner, standard supervised fine-tuning; LoRA rank 64, alpha 128 in the reported config), and ReST^EM over the dream-generation policy (outer RL: generate, filter by binary improvement reward, fine-tune on positively-rewarded generations, iterate — an EM-flavored alternative to PPO/GRPO that needs no value network). Gradient-based dream selection additionally requires one backward pass per candidate dream to compute $g_{DR}^{(i)}$ before any dream is accepted. Reported common hyperparameters (Table 5): LR $5\times 10^{-6}$, effective batch 32, 100 training steps for Sleep (vs 500 for GRPO baseline), LoRA $r=64$, $\alpha=128$. Nothing in the sleep machinery (the $\lambda, \alpha, \gamma, z_0$ knobs, the reward model, the ReST^EM loop) is itself meta-learned end-to-end at pre-training time — it is an algorithmic wrapper around a pre-trained model, which is an important contrast with Titans/ATLAS-style papers where the memory-update rule's parameters are meta-learned.
inner_loop_test_time:
At deployment the model has state changing on THREE timescales.

(A) TOKEN/CHUNK TIMESCALE (wake). The sequence layer maintains its usual state (KV cache for attention, or a fixed-size recurrent memory if a Titans-style module is used). On top of that, every CMS block $\ell$ accumulates optimizer error contributions $\eta_t^{(\ell)} f(\boldsymbol{\theta}_t^{(f_\ell)}; x_t)$ token by token and APPLIES them to its own weights once every $C^{(\ell)}$ tokens (Eq. 2). So the inference engine must (i) run a backward-like computation to get the error term per token (or per micro-chunk) for each active block and (ii) store an accumulator the size of each block's parameters. Amortized per-token cost of the update for block $\ell$ is (1 parameter-sized accumulation per token) + (1 parameter write per $C^{(\ell)}$ tokens); the experiments use frequency ladders like 1K -> 5K -> 10K tokens (Figure 7), so slow blocks touch their weights extremely rarely. This is the 'online consolidation' inherited from Nested Learning/Hope and is what the paper's wake phase runs.

(B) SLEEP TIMESCALE — CONSOLIDATION. At every step index divisible by some $C^{(\ell)}$ (i.e., at chunk boundaries $\{C^{(\ell)} \times b\}$), before block $\ell^*-1$ is updated/overwritten, the system: activates one new low-rank expert ($2\, d\, d_{low}$ parameters, $d_{low} \ll d$; the reported config adds 5 MLP blocks of dimension 64 while keeping the ACTIVE parameter count equal to the 3B/8B base) in block $\ell^*$; samples a distillation corpus $\mathcal{D}$ from the pre-expansion self; runs the $\mathcal{L}_{KS}$ optimization (GKD divergence on mixed teacher-data/on-policy rollouts + LTI prefix-completion RL with semantic + Levenshtein rewards) updating only that expert; then resets the previously-added low-rank experts of the faster block $\ell^*-1$. Per-sleep compute is dominated by autoregressive sampling (teacher corpus generation + student on-policy rollouts + LTI completions) plus forward/backward over a LoRA-sized parameter set; per-sleep persistent-state growth is one low-rank expert per consolidated pair (bounded in practice by the pre-allocated masked expert pool).

(C) SLEEP TIMESCALE — DREAMING. Generate $m$ dreams conditioned on task context $C$ with randomized extra expert routing; score each with one backward pass ($g_{DR}^{(i)} = \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}_{SFT}$); keep Top-$k$ + $b$ random; run an isolated LoRA SFT per kept dream; evaluate $\tau$; reinforce with ReST^EM. Concrete numbers from the ARC protocol: 60 dreams sampled and 45 rejected per task during sleep training; at test time on an unseen task, 5 dreams are generated and each applied INDEPENDENTLY (5 parallel LoRA-adapted model instances) before predicting, with the reported metric the fraction of dreams yielding a correct answer. This is the direct SEAL-style test-time-training inheritance: even 'inference' on a new task involves gradient updates. Efficiency accounting (App. B.5): per training step, Sleep is 4x more expensive than plain SFT; but at matched target accuracy on AIME-24/AIME-25/HMMT-25, SFT needs 4.3x/3.6x/4.8x the wall-clock of Sleep — i.e., the paradigm buys sample/step efficiency, not cheap steps.

concepts_introduced.name: Sleep paradigm (wake/sleep lifecycle)
concepts_introduced.definition: Replacement of the train/test split for continual learners: alternating 'active/wake' phases (model receives and processes new input) and 'sleep' phases (minimal/no input; internal computation consolidates memories and self-improves). Sleep = Memory Consolidation (NREM analog) + Dreaming (REM analog).

concepts_introduced.name: Online vs. offline consolidation (for neural networks)
concepts_introduced.definition: Online consolidation: knowledge transfer from fast (high-frequency) to slow (low-frequency) blocks that happens end-to-end during the wake phase (what Nested Learning/Hope already does). Offline consolidation: sleep-phase transfer using self-generated data, with lossy abstraction and capacity expansion (this paper's contribution).

concepts_introduced.name: Knowledge Seeding (KS) / upward distillation
concepts_introduced.definition: Distillation in which one or more SMALLER models (teachers) transfer knowledge into a LARGER model (student), inverting the usual KD direction so the student preserves teacher knowledge while gaining capacity.

concepts_introduced.name: Self-Knowledge Seeding (SKS)
concepts_introduced.definition: KS where teacher and student are two versions of the same model: teacher = pre-expansion state LM_theta (some parameters inactive), student = post-expansion state LM_theta_exp with newly activated parameters; used to consolidate a high-frequency block into a low-frequency block.

concepts_introduced.name: Learning to Imitate (LTI)
concepts_introduced.definition: RL add-on to distillation: sample prefixes of teacher-generated sequences, have the student complete them, reward r = gamma*r_sem + (1-gamma)*r_abs with a frozen semantic reward model (binary) and a thresholded Levenshtein-based token-level reward; teaches the student to USE (not just store) distilled knowledge by aligning sampling behavior.

concepts_introduced.name: Periodic parameter (de)activation / gradual parameter expansion
concepts_introduced.definition: At each sleep step, deactivate (reset) low-rank experts previously added to a faster block and activate a new low-rank expert {A in R^{d x d_low}, B in R^{d_low x d}} in the slower block; implemented by pre-allocating all experts and masking them until activation (static tensor shapes).

concepts_introduced.name: Dreaming (self-modifying process)
concepts_introduced.definition: REM-analog sleep stage: model generates m synthetic 'dreams' from task context C with each MoE router forcing one random extra expert (novelty injection), filters by gradient-based importance score g_DR = grad_theta L_SFT(DREAM, theta) (Top-k plus b random), LoRA-SFTs an isolated instance per dream, rewards dream generation 1/0 by downstream improvement, and optimizes the generator with ReST^EM. 'Dream' is SEAL's 'self-edit' generalized.

concepts_introduced.name: Gradient-based dream selection
concepts_introduced.definition: Rejection sampling of synthetic data by importance score equal to the gradient of the language-modeling (SFT) objective on the candidate, borrowed from gradient-based data selection (G-DIG/GREATS); keeps Top-k plus b random samples for diversity.

concepts_introduced.name: Synaptic-pruning reset
concepts_introduced.definition: After a fast block's knowledge is consolidated upward, all low-rank experts previously added to that fast block are reset to reclaim its capacity — the counterpart of biological synaptic pruning and of NREM synaptic homeostasis (downscaling).

concepts_introduced.name: Continuum Memory System (CMS) [imported from Nested Learning]
concepts_introduced.definition: A chain of MLP blocks MLP^(f_1)...MLP^(f_k) after a sequence layer, block l updated every C^(l) = max_l' C^(l') / f_l steps by accumulated optimizer error (Eq. 2); attention = infinite-frequency memory, frozen MLP = zero-frequency; the frequency spectrum realizes a short-term-to-long-term memory hierarchy.

concepts_introduced.name: Update frequency f_W (Definition 1) [imported from Nested Learning]
concepts_introduced.definition: For a weight component W, the number of its updates per unit of time, the unit being one update step of the slowest module (fast weights over length-L sequences have f = L).

assumptions_and_scope: Architectural assumptions: the full mechanism presumes a Nested-Learning/CMS backbone whose MLP blocks are sparse MoEs with routers (stated 'without loss of generality', but expansion, random-expert dreaming, and reset all lean on the MoE structure); chunk sizes are nested ($C^{(\ell)}$ divisible by $C^{(\ell-1)}$). The experiments, however, mostly GRAFT the sleep machinery onto standard backbones (Llama-3B/8B, Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen3-1.7B/8B) — e.g., 'Sleep (Transformer)' with a two-level memory system and a four-level variant — so the paper is best read as a paradigm + proof-of-concept, not a from-scratch pre-trained architecture at scale. Resource assumptions: sleep requires a frozen semantic reward model for $r_{sem}$; dreaming requires a sampled task pair $(C, \tau)$, i.e., a context AND a downstream performance measure available during sleep — task-aware sleep, which limits fully task-free deployment; ReST^EM and per-dream LoRA SFT require training infrastructure to be reachable from the serving environment. Scale/scope limits: backbones are 1B-8B; additional parameters are small (5 MLP blocks of dim 64) with active parameter count held equal to the base; most results are presented as figures (Figures 3-6) without full numeric tables; Tables 1-3 in the extraction are partially interleaved, though the headline numbers are recoverable; there is no from-scratch large-scale pre-training, no wall-clock breakdown of an end-to-end wake/sleep cycle at serving scale, and no safety analysis of recursive self-modification. Provenance caveat: the paper notes a version has been on OpenReview since September 2025 and uses this to claim priority over the 2026 OPSD wave discussed in Appendix A.4.
experiments_and_scale: Backbones: Llama-3B and Llama3-8B (class-incremental), Llama-3.2-1B (ARC), Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-8B (math reasoning), plus Hope-architecture variants; additional parameters = 5 MLP blocks of dimension 64, active parameter count unchanged from the 3B/8B base. Training config (Table 5): LR 5e-6, effective batch 32, 100 steps (Sleep/SFT) vs 500 (GRPO), LoRA r=64 alpha=128. (1) Class-incremental learning (CLINC150: 150 intents/10 domains/23.7K queries; Banking77: 77 intents/13,083 examples; DBpedia level-2, 70 classes, 10K train/1K test): Hope + memory consolidation beats ICL, EWC, InCA, and plain Hope across all three (Figure 3; consolidation converts prompt-level adaptation into durable parametric memory). (2) Long-context / effect of number of sleep levels (MK-NIAH from RULER, LongHealth 20 cases x ~5-7K words / 200 questions, QASPER ~5K questions over 1.6K papers): Hope variants beat ICL, DuoAttention, and Cartridges; more consolidation stages monotonically help; making the most persistent (lowest-frequency) memory MORE adaptive hurts retention (Figure 4). (3) Continual Translation of a Novel Language (MTOB/Kalamang + Manchu, ChRF): under sequential learning ICL collapses to near pre-trained behavior while Hope-1/2/3 retain gains, monotone in number of consolidation stages; Hope-3 nearly recovers single-language performance; Cartridges and SFT catastrophically forget at least one language, falling off the plot (Figure 5). (4) BABILong: Hope (Sleep) stays near-perfect up to 10M tokens, while GPT-4/GPT-4o-mini fail beyond 128K-256K, Llama-8B+RAG degrades with length, and fine-tuned Titans/ARMT/RMT degrade sharply past ~1M (Figure 6); all small models need fine-tuning to compress ultra-long contexts. (5) Math reasoning (avg@16 on AIME-24 / AIME-25 / HMMT-25): Qwen3-1.7B: Base 49.8/34.5/25.7, SFT 47.3/36.1/22.9, GRPO 51.0/38.6/26.1, OPSD 51.6/40.0/28.1, Sleep 53.2/40.2/29.3. Qwen3-8B: Base 73.8, SFT 75.5, GRPO 76.4, OPSD 76.6, Sleep 79.2 on AIME-24, with Sleep also best on AIME-25 (69.0) and HMMT-25 (46.1); the 8B base rows for AIME-25/HMMT-25 are interleaved in the extraction (approx. 66-68 / 42-45 range). Ablations (Qwen3-8B, Table 1): full Sleep 79.2/69.0/46.1; minus Imitation Learning 76.8/67.9/45.0; minus Semantic Reward 78.9/69.2/44.5; without Expansion 78.2/67.9/44.9; OPSD 76.6/67.4/45.1; OPSD+Expansion 77.9/68.2/45.9 — every component contributes. (6) Knowledge incorporation (SQuAD no-context accuracy, SEAL protocol): single passage n=1: Base 31.9, FT-no-dreaming 33.4, SEAL 46.7, Sleep(Transformer, 2-level) 48.1, Sleep(Transformer, 4-level) 48.9; continued pretraining n=200 passages / 974 questions, 5 dreams per passage aggregated: 31.9 / 32.0 / 43.2 / 44.3 / 46.2. Dreaming ablations (n=1 / n=200): remove gradient-based selection 47.1/45.2, remove random expert 48.0/44.7, remove Dreaming entirely 35.7/36.2 — dreaming is the dominant factor here. (7) Few-shot ARC (Llama-3.2-1B, 11 train / 8 held-out tasks; 60 dreams sampled, 45 rejected per task; 5 dreams applied independently at test): ICL 0%, TTT+synthetic-updates 10%, SEAL 72.5%, Sleep 80%. (8) Efficiency (App. B.5): per step Sleep costs 4x SFT, but to REACH Sleep's accuracy SFT needs 4.3x/3.6x/4.8x more wall-clock on AIME-24/AIME-25/HMMT-25 respectively.
systems_implications: (1) Inference is no longer forward-only. The wake phase of a CMS backbone requires computing an optimizer error term per token per active MLP block and applying accumulated updates every $C^{(\ell)}$ tokens — the serving engine needs backward-capable kernels and parameter-sized accumulators resident next to the weights, with update cadences like 1K/5K/10K tokens (Figure 7). Because parameters are constant within a chunk, chunk-level batching/parallelism is preserved (the same property TNT, arXiv:2511.07343, exploits for training); the writes themselves are rare and amortized. (2) State-size math changes category. In a pure Transformer, session state = KV cache, O(L) — at BABILong's 10M tokens this is untenable (GPT-4-class models fail past 128-256K). Here the sequence layer can be fixed-state and the durable session state becomes PARAMETERS: per consolidation, one low-rank expert of $2\,d\,d_{low}$ values ($d_{low} \ll d$; experiments add 5 dim-64 blocks total while holding active parameters constant). That is a per-user/per-agent weight-delta serving problem (multi-tenant LoRA-style adapter serving, versioning, eviction), not a KV-cache problem. (3) Static shapes by design. The masked pre-allocation trick (all prospective experts exist from t=0, masked until activated) deliberately avoids tensor resizing, so compiled graphs, kernel autotuning, and checkpoint formats stay stable; the price is dead weights/FLOPs for unactivated experts unless the runtime skips masked experts in routing (sparse MoE dispatch makes this natural). (4) Sleep is a scheduled offline training job attached to a serving deployment: teacher-corpus sampling + on-policy student rollouts (generation-heavy, inference-shaped), LTI RL with a reward-model service plus cheap Levenshtein scoring, one backward pass PER candidate dream for gradient-based selection (60 dreams -> 60 backward passes per ARC task), and per-dream isolated LoRA SFT jobs that are embarrassingly parallel, then ReST^EM iterations. Infra-wise this couples serving fleets to fine-tuning capacity on a recurring schedule, and every sleep produces a NEW model version — checkpoint management, cache invalidation, regression testing, and rollback become continuous-operation concerns rather than release-time ones. (5) Cost profile: Sleep steps cost ~4x SFT steps, but iso-accuracy Sleep is 3.6-4.8x cheaper in wall-clock than SFT — i.e., for a fixed capability target the paradigm is compute-favorable, but it front-loads complexity (RL, reward model, MoE growth bookkeeping). (6) Test-time inference for new tasks (ARC protocol) itself spawns 5 dream-adapted model instances — fan-out serving with per-instance LoRA deltas, with gradient updates in the serving loop.
connections: WITHIN THE SIX-PAPER SET, this is the capstone that stacks a lifecycle on top of the architecture line: Titans (arXiv:2501.00663) introduced the deep neural long-term memory updated at test time by surprise/momentum/decay and appears here as a BABILong baseline that degrades past ~1M tokens where Hope+Sleep does not; Miras / 'It's All Connected' (arXiv:2504.13173) supplied the view of sequence models as online optimization of an attentional-bias objective with retention gates, which is the conceptual backdrop for calling every block 'a memory with an update rule'; ATLAS (arXiv:2505.23735) pushed optimal test-time memorization (Omega rule, sliding windows, Muon-style second-order updates) for the sequence layer this paper treats as a black-box short-term memory; TNT (arXiv:2511.07343) provides the chunkwise-training machinery that makes multi-frequency test-time memorization efficient — precisely the Eq.-2 chunk structure Sleep schedules around; and Nested Learning (arXiv:2512.24695) is the direct parent: it contributes the CMS, Definition 1's update-frequency formalism, the Hope architecture, the anterograde-amnesia framing, and 'online consolidation', of which this paper builds the missing 'offline' half. EXTERNAL LINEAGE: fast weight programmers (Schmidhuber 1992) supply the canonical frequency example and the self-modification theme (also Schmidhuber 1987 and the self-referential weight matrix, Irie et al. 2022); TTT (Sun et al. 2024) and linear attention (Katharopoulos et al. 2020) / Mamba (Gu & Dao 2023) / xLSTM appear as the 'learning to compress' architectures whose fixed-size states motivate the short-term side; SEAL (Zweiger et al. 2025) is the substrate for Dreaming (self-edits -> dreams; same binary reward and ReST^EM, Singh et al. 2024), improved by consolidation-first ordering, gradient-based dream selection (G-DIG, GREATS), and random-expert novelty; GKD (Agarwal et al. 2024) is the distillation backbone of Knowledge Seeding; Cartridges (Eyuboglu et al. 2025) and sleep-time compute (Lin et al. 2025) are the closest prior 'offline processing' systems, distinguished because they compress into KV/text space while Sleep distills into parametric weight space; EWC (Kirkpatrick 2017) and InCA represent the regularization/external-learner continual-learning alternatives it beats. Appendix A.4 maps the concurrent 2026 on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) wave (OPSD, On-Policy Context Distillation, GATES, SD-Zero, COPSD, SDFT, OEL, pi-Play, CRISP, MTP, OPSDL, Skill-SD, MSD) and differentiates Sleep on four axes: upward distillation into newly grown capacity (vs re-conditioning a fixed teacher), a chain of frequency-ordered memories (vs a flat teacher/student pair), a two-phase sleep including Dreaming (vs consolidation only), and GKD+imitation-learning (vs pure per-token reverse-KL) — citing OPSD failure modes (epistemic-verbalization suppression with up to 40% OOD drops, Kim et al. 2026; leakage/collapse under iteration) as motivation for the two-stage design. WHAT IT LEAVES OPEN: the sleep machinery is grafted onto pre-trained backbones rather than co-trained; when/how often to sleep is fixed by the chunk schedule rather than learned; dreaming needs an explicit task pair (C, tau); and capacity growth, though bounded by pre-allocation, has no principled budget or forgetting-vs-growth theory.
open_questions: (1) Scale and end-to-end validation: all results are 1B-8B with small added parameter budgets and 100-step sleep optimizations; nothing shows the paradigm co-trained from scratch or run over many wake/sleep cycles of a long deployed life — does repeated expansion+reset stay stable over hundreds of sleeps, and does the pre-allocated expert pool eventually exhaust? (2) Scheduling: sleep times are hard-wired to chunk boundaries $\{C^{(\ell)} \times b\}$; can the model learn WHEN to sleep, and what happens under irregular real-world traffic? (3) Task-free dreaming: the dreaming loop requires a sampled $(C, \tau)$ — a context and an evaluable downstream measure — during sleep; fully unsupervised deployment has no $\tau$, so what replaces the binary improvement reward? (4) Reward-model dependence: $r_{sem}$ uses a frozen external reward model — its biases and drift over a continually-changing student are unexamined, and the semantic-reward ablation is actually BETTER on AIME-25 (69.2 vs 69.0), suggesting the component is not uniformly helpful. (5) Router dynamics: how the MoE router learns to dispatch to newly activated experts (and to stop dispatching to reset ones) is never specified — a real implementation gap. (6) Systems accounting: no wall-clock or energy breakdown of a full sleep cycle at serving scale, no analysis of the 60-backward-passes-per-task dream-selection cost, and no comparison against a simple replay-buffer baseline at matched compute. (7) Theory: CF is reframed as a capacity problem, but there is no formal statement of how much capacity per consolidation prevents how much forgetting, nor of what the lossy 'abstraction' in upward distillation preserves. (8) Safety/governance of recursive self-modification (models rewriting their own weights nightly, with random-expert novelty injection) is not discussed at all. (9) Presentation gaps a careful reader must flag: several headline results exist only as figures; Tables 1-3 are typeset interleaved (the Qwen3-8B base row is ambiguous in the extraction); and the near-perfect 10M-token BABILong claim relies on fine-tuning all small models, so the zero-shot picture is much weaker. FOR THE STUDY PAPER'S TRAINING-NAIVE AUDIENCE, sections needing background scaffolding: knowledge distillation and KL-divergence objectives (forward vs reverse, on-policy vs off-policy), policy-gradient RL and ReST^EM/GRPO at a working level, LoRA and adapter-based fine-tuning, MoE routing, catastrophic forgetting and EWC, and what 'backpropagating through an inner update' means — every sleep-phase equation presumes these.
